## Exams {#exams}

Two exams, each worth 25 points (5% of your grade). Both are taken in the **testing center**
on your own schedule within the posted window. Both are closed book, proctored, and
multiple choice.

Almost everything else you submit in this course is built with AI assistance, and that is
the point. These two sittings are the exception. They are the one place your own
understanding is measured on its own, which is why they exist and why they are worth
holding yourself to.

They are also deliberately low stakes. At 5% each, the difference between a rough exam and
a strong one is about two percent of your course grade. That is enough to make preparing
worth it and not enough for one bad morning to matter.

### Midterm Exam {#midterm-exam}

**25 points | Testing center, Oct 20 to 26 | 40 items**

Covers classes 1 through 6: the Agentic Workflow, Discovery, and Design axes.

### Final Exam {#final-exam}

**25 points | Testing center, Dec 14 to 17 | 60 items**

Cumulative across all six axes, ten items per axis. Because the item count is even across
axes, your score comes back as a six-sided profile you can compare against the self
assessment you filled out in week 1 and again in week 13. The gap between what you think you
know and what you can produce under proctoring is usually the most useful thing on the page.

Questions are application rather than recall. Expect "which of these is a leading indicator
for this product" rather than "define leading indicator." Reading the chapters is the
preparation; skimming them is not.

## Sprints

Six sprints, two weeks each. Sprints 1 through 5 are worth 50 points. Sprint 6 is worth 100.
From Sprint 2 on, each sprint is two Canvas assignments: the **Plan** (10 points, due the first
Wednesday) and the **Wrap-up** (40 points, or 90 for Sprint 6, due the day the sprint ends).

Every sprint is the same assignment: same structure, same deliverables, same rubric. What
changes is what you decide to work on. A sprint is a timebox, not a phase.

You are not all building the same kind of thing. Some of you are building your own product.
Some of you are on a team and are working on whatever your role covers. The requirements
below apply to both, and the rubric is the same for both.

### What you turn in, and how

Every sprint has the same four deliverables.

| Deliverable | What it is | Where it lives | How you turn it in | When | Points |
|---|---|---|---|---|--:|
| **Plan** | What you will do, why, how you will know it is done, and how hard you expect it to be. `/sprint-plan` helps you write it. | `sprints/sprint-N-plan.md` in your course repo | Commit it, and paste its GitHub link into **Sprint N Plan** on Canvas | First Wednesday, 11:59 PM | 10 |
| **Shipped** | The work itself: real, finished, and reachable by someone else | Your course repo, another repo, or a live link | Nothing separate to submit. List every place it lives under **Where the work lives** in your README | Last day | 20 |
| **Review** | What `/sprint-review` produces: a report on your sprint, then your answers to its five retro questions | `sprints/sprint-N-review.md` in your course repo | Commit it, and paste its GitHub link into **Sprint N Wrap-up** on Canvas | Last day | 10 |
| **Demo** | 60 to 90 seconds on Loom of the work, working | Loom | Paste the Loom share link into **Sprint N Wrap-up** on Canvas | Last day | 10 |

**Retro**, short for retrospective, is your part of the review: your answers to the five
questions `/sprint-review` asks after it shows you the report. Did you hit the goal, what did
the report show you, why did the plan change if it did, how hard was it really, and what will you
change next sprint. It saves your answers word for word with the report.

Sprint 6 is worth 100: Plan 10, Shipped 50, Review 20, Demo 20.

### How every sprint works

#### Day one

Run `/sprint-plan`. It asks you what you are going to do and writes `sprints/sprint-N-plan.md`:

```markdown
# Sprint N Plan

**Goal:** What will be true in two weeks that is not true now?

**Why this:** Why is this the right next thing?

**Done looks like:** How will you know the goal was met? Be specific enough
that someone else could check.

**Predicted difficulty:** 1 to 5.
```

**Submit it on Canvas by Wednesday, 11:59 PM.** Commit and push the file, then paste its GitHub
link into that sprint's Plan assignment. On time, with Goal, Why this, Done looks like, and
Predicted difficulty all filled in, earns all 10 points. You do not resubmit when the plan
changes: the link always shows the current file.

**You can change the plan.** Plans change once you learn something, and that is normal. Edit the
file and add a line saying what changed and why:

```markdown
**Changes:** Sep 24: dropped the slide template and added a competitor benchmark, because the
licensing research had to come first.
```

Changes cost nothing. At the end, your work is read against the plan as it stands, and your
retro says how it moved. A change with no note is the one thing to avoid: without it, nobody
reading your plan can tell what you set out to do.

#### The two weeks

Do the work, in your repo.

#### The last day

**1. Run `/sprint-review`.** It shows you every project you worked in during the sprint window
and asks which ones were this sprint. It then reads those sessions and your commits and writes
a report: when you worked, where you got stuck and how you got unstuck, what took the most time,
and which of the six axes your work advanced. It reads only the projects you confirm, and
nothing leaves your machine except the report.

**2. Answer its five retro questions.** After showing you the report, `/sprint-review` asks:

1. Did you hit the goal? Yes, partly, or no, and why.
2. What did the report show you that you didn't expect, or wouldn't have noticed yourself?
3. If the plan changed, why?
4. Actual difficulty, 1 to 5, and why it differed from what you predicted.
5. What will you change next sprint?

Answer in your own words. It saves your answers exactly as you write them at the bottom of
`sprints/sprint-N-review.md`, then commits and pushes the file.

**3. Record a 60 to 90 second demo on [Loom](https://www.loom.com).** Show the thing working, with real content. No slides, no intro,
no reflection. A minute or so of the actual thing. Loom only: not Google Drive, YouTube, or an uploaded
file. Submit the Loom share link. A demo that is not a Loom scores 0.

**4. Submit two links in that sprint's Wrap-up assignment on Canvas:** your review file on
GitHub (`sprints/sprint-N-review.md`, with your retro at the bottom) and your Loom demo. Before
you do, make sure the **Where the work lives** section of your README lists every repo and live
link someone would need to check what you shipped. Sprint 1 was one Canvas assignment and asked
for your repo URL instead.

### What you have to have

- **You shipped something.** It exists now, it did not two weeks ago, and someone other than
  you can reach it, use it, or see it.
- **Someone can check it.** It is in your course repo, in another repo listed in your README
  (shared with us if you can), or live at a link. Work nobody can check, anywhere, does not
  count as shipped.
- **The plan,** submitted on Canvas by Wednesday, committed, and kept current with any changes
  noted.
- **The review,** committed: the `/sprint-review` report with your answers to its five retro
  questions at the bottom.
- **The Loom demo, 60 to 90 seconds.**

### What "shipped" means for different work

Not every sprint produces code. What counts is that the thing is real and someone else can
reach it, use it, or see it.

| If your sprint was | Shipped means |
|---|---|
| A product feature | Deployed and working in the live app |
| Frontend or design work | The new interface is live, not a mockup |
| A landing page or campaign | The page is published at a URL |
| Pricing or financial modeling | The model exists, runs on real numbers, and your team can use it |
| Marketing or sales copy | The copy is published or in use, not sitting in a doc |
| An automation or workflow | It runs, and you can show it running |
| Research or discovery | The findings are written up in your repo and someone acted on them |
| Analytics or measurement | The tracking is live and returning real data |

If your work does not fit any of these, say what shipping means for it in your plan file before
the sprint starts.

#### Any real artifact counts

Your sprint can advance any of the six axes, and every one produces artifacts. Code is one kind
among many. Any digital artifact that reflects real work counts, in whatever format it
naturally takes:

| Axis | Artifacts that count, for example |
|---|---|
| Agentic Workflow | A `CLAUDE.md`, slash commands and skills, subagent setups, specs, an automation that runs |
| Discovery | Interview notes and synthesis, personas, a problem statement, survey results, a competitive teardown |
| Design | Flows, wireframes and mockups, a Figma file, a usability test write-up, a live interface |
| Application Architecture | Code, a deployed app on Vercel or elsewhere, a data model, an API, tests |
| AI Systems | Prompts in the product, an eval set and its results, a working model call |
| Launch and Learn | A landing page, a pitch deck, pricing or a financial model, sales copy, an analytics dashboard |

Markdown files, Word documents, slide decks, spreadsheets, PDFs, images, and live links are all
fine. Two tests apply to every one of them: it is real work (not a template or a placeholder),
and someone else can open it. Commit it to a repo or list its link under **Where the work
lives** in your README; for a Google Doc, Figma file, or anything else that lives behind a link,
make sure the link opens for us.

Interview notes and recordings are about real people. Commit notes and synthesis with names
removed, and keep recordings out of the repo.

### The difficulty scale

| | |
|---|---|
| **1** | I already know how to do this |
| **2** | I know most of it, with a few small gaps to fill |
| **3** | I will have to learn something new, but the path is clear |
| **4** | I will have to learn a lot, and the path is not clear |
| **5** | I do not know whether this is possible |

Difficulty is not graded in either direction. Rate it honestly.

### Grading rubric

50 points, or 100 for Sprint 6. The same four categories every sprint. The Plan assignment is
the first category; the Wrap-up assignment is the other three.

| Category | Points | Sprint 6 | What earns full marks |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| **Plan** | 10 | 10 | Its GitHub link submitted on Canvas by Wednesday, 11:59 PM, with Goal, Why this, Done looks like, and Predicted difficulty all filled in. Graded for completion. |
| **Shipped** | 20 | 50 | Real, finished, and someone else can reach it, use it, or see it. Read against your plan as it stands at the end, and weighed by how hard the work was for you. |
| **Review** | 10 | 20 | Report committed, with your retro answering all five questions and responding to something specific in the report. |
| **Demo** | 10 | 20 | 60 to 90 seconds on Loom, the real thing, working, with real content. A demo that is not a Loom scores 0. |

The plan is graded for completion, and your predicted difficulty is not graded. Aim high.
From Sprint 2 on, "shipped" is weighed by how hard the work actually was for you, judged from
the work itself: an ambitious goal you partly reach and
account for in your retro can still earn full marks, and routine work you comfortably finish
earns up to 15 of 20.

**Questions about your sprint feedback** go only to the Course Monitor app in the course Slack:
send it a direct message saying what you think was missed. Professor Murff reviews every message
sent there. Questions sent by email or anywhere else may be missed.

### Confidential company work

Many of you build inside a company whose code, data, or customers are not yours alone to share.
You never have to share a company repo. Any of these works:

- Share the repo with Professor Murff (`sdmurff`) if you and your
  team are comfortable with that. Your course repo can stay private either way.
- Leave it unshared and list it under **Where the work lives** in your README. `/sprint-review`
  reads its commit history on your own computer and puts a summary in your report: dates,
  messages, and file names, never code.
- Show the result instead: the live product, a store listing, an account for the graders, or
  your Loom. For most work that is the strongest evidence anyway.
- If none of that works, build a sanitized version with fake data and note it in your plan file.

Nothing in this course has to be public.

### Sprint 1 {#sprint-1}

**50 points | Assigned: Mon, Sep 14 | Due: Mon, Sep 28**

**Sprint 1 plan due: Wed, Sep 16, 11:59 PM.**

The standard sprint, plus two one-time items:

1. **Your repo,** created from the [builder template](https://github.com/byu-strategy/builder-template), with Professor Murff (`sdmurff`) added as a collaborator.
2. **A context declaration** in that repo's `README.md`: your role (most roles combine several
   hats), what you are working on, who it is for, and who uses your work. "Not decided" is
   fine to start; choosing is a legitimate Sprint 1 goal. Later sprints are read against this.
   Revise it when it changes and note why.

#### Set up with Claude Code

A prompt walks you through all of it in Claude Code: creating your repo, adding the
collaborators, writing your context declaration, and committing your Sprint 1 plan. Claude
explains each step as it goes. Plan on about an hour.

1. Finish [Computer Setup](00-computer-setup.qmd) through step 6, and know your GitHub username.
2. Make a folder for class projects, such as `Documents/projects`. Avoid folders synced by
   OneDrive, iCloud, Google Drive, or Dropbox.
3. In VS Code, choose **File > Open Folder** and open that folder. Choose **Terminal > New
   Terminal**, type `claude`, and press Enter.
4. Expand the prompt below, click the copy button, paste it into Claude, and press Enter.

Partway through, Claude asks you to reopen VS Code inside your new repo folder and paste the
same prompt again. That is expected: it checks what is already done and picks up there.

**If you get stuck,** post your question in the [course Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/byustrategyprogram/shared_invite/zt-49zknsqc4-iJK8onSDn5ZqKLnaasHXQA). Include the last error message Claude showed you and the task number you were on.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Setup prompt: paste into Claude Code"}
```bash
I am a student in MSB 341 Product Management at BYU. Help me set up my course repo and write
my first sprint plan. I may be new to git, GitHub, and the terminal, so teach me what is going
on as we go.

Deadline: Wednesday, September 16, 2026, 11:59 PM Mountain Time. The assignment is complete
when sprints/sprint-1-plan.md is visible in my repo on GitHub.

COURSE FACTS
- Template repo: byu-strategy/builder-template
- My repo: named <my NetID in lowercase>_msb341, owned by my personal GitHub account, private
- Collaborator to add: sdmurff (instructor)

HOW TO WORK WITH ME
- First do CHECK FIRST below. Then make a task list from TASKS, mark anything already done as
  complete, and show it to me. Update the list as tasks finish and show it at the end of each
  task.
- One task at a time. Before each task, explain in two or three plain sentences what we are
  about to do and why. Define terms like repository, clone, commit, and push the first time
  they come up.
- Show each command before you run it and say in one sentence what it does. Run commands
  yourself unless a task says I have to.
- When you need something from me (a login, a choice, an answer), stop and wait.
- End each task with a one-sentence recap of what changed.
- If something fails, explain the error in plain language and fix it if you can. If you
  cannot, tell me exactly what to post in the course Slack, and give me the link:
  https://join.slack.com/t/byustrategyprogram/shared_invite/zt-49zknsqc4-iJK8onSDn5ZqKLnaasHXQA
- Keep explanations short.

CHECK FIRST (every time this prompt is pasted)
I may paste this prompt twice: once in my projects folder and again inside my repo folder.
Before making the task list, check:
1. My operating system.
2. Whether this folder is a git repo, and if so which GitHub repo it points to (git remote -v).
3. Whether git and gh are installed, and whether gh is logged in (gh auth status).
4. If gh is logged in: my GitHub username, whether my repo exists and is private, which of
   sdmurff is a collaborator or has a pending invitation, and whether
   sprints/sprint-1-plan.md exists in my repo on GitHub.
Ask for my NetID if you need it. Tell me in a few lines what is already done.

TASKS

1. Check this folder.
   Make sure the current folder is not inside OneDrive, iCloud Drive, Google Drive, or
   Dropbox, because sync tools can corrupt git repos. If this folder is a git repo that is not
   my own repo (for example byu-strategy/builder-template, cloned in class), explain that it
   is the class's shared copy: I cannot push to it, and pointing it at my repo will not work
   because the two have separate histories. Ask whether I changed any files in it; if I did,
   remember its path for task 4. Then have me open a different folder, start claude, and paste
   this prompt again.

2. Install the tools.
   Explain that git tracks versions of files and gh lets us work with GitHub from the
   terminal. If git is missing: on a Mac, have me run xcode-select --install and wait for it;
   on Windows, send me to https://git-scm.com. If gh is missing: on a Mac with Homebrew, run
   brew install gh; on Windows, run winget install --id GitHub.cli --source winget. Otherwise
   send me to https://cli.github.com to download the installer. Do not install Homebrew and do
   not use sudo. If an install needs a new terminal to take effect, tell me to quit VS Code
   fully, reopen it in this folder, start claude, and paste this prompt again.

3. Log in to GitHub.
   Explain that this connects the terminal to my GitHub account so pushes are allowed. I have
   to run the login myself because it asks questions. Tell me to open a second terminal with
   the + button in the terminal panel and run:
     gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web
   Tell me to copy the one-time code, press Enter, paste the code in the browser, and approve,
   and to answer Y if asked "Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?". When I say I am
   done, run gh auth setup-git, then gh auth status, and confirm I am logged in.

4. Create my repo from the template.
   Explain what a template is, why each student gets their own copy, and why it is private.
   Ask for my NetID. If the repo already exists, skip creating it. Otherwise run:
     gh repo create <netid>_msb341 --template byu-strategy/builder-template --private --clone
   If the repo exists but is not in this folder, run gh repo clone <netid>_msb341. Check that
   the new folder contains CLAUDE.md and a sprints folder. If the folder is empty, delete that
   empty folder and run gh repo clone <netid>_msb341. If the repo is public, make it private
   with gh repo edit <username>/<netid>_msb341 --visibility private
   --accept-visibility-change-consequences. If task 1 found files I changed in a class copy,
   copy those files (never the .git folder) into the new repo folder now.

5. Share my repo with the instructors.
   Explain that collaborators can see the repo, which is how my work reaches the instructors;
   there is nothing separate to submit. Run:
     gh api -X PUT repos/<username>/<netid>_msb341/collaborators/sdmurff
   Confirm it appears as a collaborator or a pending invitation. Pending is fine.

6. Move into my repo.
   Explain that Claude Code loads the repo's CLAUDE.md and the course commands /sprint-plan
   and /sprint-review only when it is started inside the repo folder. Tell me exactly what to
   do: type /exit, choose File > Open Folder in VS Code and open the <netid>_msb341 folder,

7. Describe my role and my work.
   Explain that README.md is the front page of the repo, that its Context section is the
   record later sprints are graded against, and that /sprint-plan reads it. Explain that it is
   expected to change as my work changes, and that the Sprint 1 version is due with Sprint 1 on
   Monday, September 28. Explain that students in this course play different roles and not
   everyone ships software, but everyone uses Claude Code to produce real work. In README.md,
   replace [your name] with my name. Then ask me about the Context section one item at a time:
   - My role, first. Most roles in this course combine several hats, so press me on it. If I
     give a one-word title like "PM" or "marketing", ask what I will actually do week to week,
     what my team needs that nobody else covers, and which parts of the work I will own. If I
     am solo, I likely wear most of the hats; ask which ones I expect to spend the most time
     on. Offer these as ideas and ask which apply:
       product: discovery, user interviews, specs, prioritization
       engineering: building features, data, deployment
       design: flows, interface, testing with users
       go-to-market: positioning, landing pages, campaigns, sales outreach
       pricing and business model: pricing research, financial models
       analytics: metrics, tracking, reporting
       operations: agent workflows and automations that do repetitive work
     The ideas are prompts, not answers. Do not assign me a role. Record the hats I choose, in
     my words.
   - What I am working on: my own product, or my part of a team's product. If I do not know
     yet, write "Not decided" followed by the options I am weighing, and tell me that choosing
     is a legitimate Sprint 1 goal.
   - Who it is for: the customer or segment the work ultimately serves.
   - Who uses my work: the specific person who will use what I make. For a team role this can
     be my teammates, such as engineers using my specs or sales using my pricing.
   Mark anything I cannot answer yet as "Not decided". Use my words; tighten them, but do not
   invent a role, a project, or answers for me. Then explain commit and push, commit with the
   message "Add project context", push, and confirm it went to <username>/<netid>_msb341.

8. Write my Sprint 1 plan.
   Explain that each sprint is two weeks and opens with a plan submitted on Canvas by
   Wednesday, that the plan is graded for completion, and that the predicted difficulty is not

   and follow its instructions exactly. The answers must be mine: do not suggest a goal for

9. Confirm it is turned in.

   the repo is private, and that sdmurff is a collaborator or invited. Show the
   finished task list and a short summary: my repo URL, the deadline, and that every sprint

RULES
- Never write my README answers or my sprint plan for me.
- Never push to any repo other than <username>/<netid>_msb341.
- Never ask for, show, or store passwords or tokens.
- No real names, emails, or phone numbers of other people go in the repo.
- Change git and gh settings only as these tasks require.
```

## Peer Assignments

Peer assignments teach you to give and receive constructive feedback, a critical professional skill. You'll be randomly paired with different classmates for each assignment.

---

### Peer Code Review

**50 points | Assigned: Mon, Nov 2 | Due: Mon, Nov 9**

**Goal:** Apply code analysis skills to a peer's codebase and provide constructive feedback.

**Process:**

1. You'll be assigned a partner (different from your product testing partner)
2. Your partner shares their GitHub repo with you
3. You use Claude Code to analyze their codebase
4. You write a professional code review
5. You actually run and test their app

**Deliverables:**

**Part 1: AI-Assisted Analysis**

Run the following prompts in Claude Code on your peer's repo and save the outputs:

```markdown
Prompt 1: "Analyze this project structure. List all directories and their purposes,
identify frontend vs backend files, and count total lines of code.
Save as peer-review-structure.md"

Prompt 2: "Trace the main user flow from UI to database.
What happens when a user performs the core action?
Save as peer-review-dataflow.md"

Prompt 3: "Identify the architecture pattern, code organization,
and any potential security concerns or code smells.
Save as peer-review-architecture.md"
```

**Part 2: Written Review**

Write a 1-2 page review covering:

- **Architecture observations:** What patterns did you notice? How is the code organized?
- **Code quality:** What's done well? What could be cleaner?
- **Security considerations:** Any obvious vulnerabilities?
- **3 specific suggestions:** Actionable improvements with rationale

**Part 3: Kick the Tires**

- Sign up and use the app as a real user
- Document: Did it work? What broke? What was confusing?

**Turn in:**

Make a copy of the [Peer Code Review submission template](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1zJvmAGrGa5NdCZDLVCl6d2tGngZzgUKooLVv-FHfO6c/copy) and fill in each section. All deliverables go in this single document:

- The 3 AI-generated analysis outputs (pasted into the template)
- Your written review covering architecture, code quality, security, and 3 specific suggestions
- Notes from your hands-on testing session

Submit the link to your completed Google Doc on Learning Suite.

**Grading Rubric (50 points)**

| Category | Points |
|----------|--------|
| AI analysis files complete and thorough | 15 |
| Written review professional and constructive | 20 |
| Testing notes with specific observations | 10 |
| Tone is helpful, not harsh | 5 |

::: {.callout-tip title="Code Review Mindset"}
Your goal is to help your peer improve, not to criticize. Frame feedback as "Have you considered..." or "One thing that might help..." Great code reviewers make others want to work with them.
:::

### Peer Product Testing

**50 points | Assigned: Mon, Nov 30 | Due: Mon, Dec 7**

**Goal:** Be a real test user for a peer's product and provide actionable UX feedback.

**Process:**

1. You'll be assigned a different partner than code review
2. You become an actual user of their product
3. You sign up, use core features, and try to break things
4. You record the whole thing

**Deliverable:** A 5-minute Loom video of you using your peer's product. That's it.

**How to record your test session:**

1. **Start Loom, share your screen, and open their app URL**
2. **Think out loud the entire time** — narrate what you see, what you expect, where you're confused, what works
3. **Try to complete the core task** — sign up, use the main feature, see if your data persists
4. **Try to break things** — what happens with bad input? Edge cases? Unexpected flows?
5. **End with your summary** — look at the camera and give:
   - 3 things that worked well (be specific)
   - 3 things you'd improve (most impactful first)
   - Would you use this product? Why or why not?

**Submit:** Your Loom URL on Canvas. Share the video with your peer too — this is a gift to them.

**Grading Rubric (50 points)**

| Score | What the TA sees |
|-------|-----------------|
| **45-50** | Genuine engagement — spent real time exploring the product. Think-aloud narration is specific and continuous. Summary feedback is actionable and constructive. |
| **35-44** | Good test session but narration is sparse, or summary feedback is vague. Clearly used the product but didn't dig deep. |
| **25-34** | Surface-level engagement. Quick walkthrough without much exploration or thoughtful feedback. |
| **15-24** | Video submitted but minimal effort. Barely used the product. |
| **0** | Not submitted. |

::: {.callout-tip title="Testing Mindset"}
Your job is to help your peer see their product through fresh eyes. Be honest but kind. The best feedback is specific ("The button on the checkout page didn't respond when I clicked it") not vague ("The checkout was buggy").
:::
